part_title: CloudFront Caching Versus Replication and Custom Origin Security

scenes.title: CloudFront caching versus S3 replication
scenes.visual_overview: Edge TTL-based caching worldwide versus S3 replication to chosen Regions; propagation, storage, update and use cases differ.
visual_walkthrough: Compare a CloudFront edge-cache copy and a regional S3 object replica as two distinct resources
Follow TTL and cache miss behavior versus independently configured S3 replication between Regions
Explain update propagation, storage charges and different resilience guarantees
scenes.visual_example: A global photo application uses CloudFront for worldwide read delivery while maintaining an S3 replica in another Region for recovery and data placement.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Caching is an optimization for reading through an edge; replication creates another regional storage copy.
scenes.narration: This two-column comparison separates CloudFront caching from S3 replication. On the CloudFront side, a viewer requests an object from a nearby edge. A valid cached copy can be returned until its time-to-live expires or a policy causes revalidation. A cache miss reaches the configured origin, so cached objects are not guaranteed independent recovery copies. On the S3 side, replication is configured to write additional object versions to a selected destination bucket, perhaps in another Region. That is a data placement and resilience decision with asynchronous delivery, its own permissions and storage charges. Imagine a photo service with users worldwide. CloudFront improves read delivery, while cross-Region S3 replication can protect against a regional failure if properly tested. Neither service automatically provides the other's function. Decide separately whether the workload needs lower-latency reads, data residency or a usable remote recovery copy.

scenes.title: ALB and EC2 custom origin reachability
scenes.visual_overview: Publicly reachable CloudFront custom origin endpoint; ALB can route to private EC2 targets; security group and origin request protocol.
visual_walkthrough: Trace CloudFront to an internet-facing ALB before reaching EC2 targets in private subnets
Separate the public origin endpoint from private target reachability
Compare the alternative of a publicly reachable EC2 custom origin and its security obligations
scenes.visual_example: A web application places private EC2 instances behind an internet-facing ALB used as the custom origin, with appropriately restricted listener access.
scenes.visual_synthesis: An ordinary custom origin must be reachable by CloudFront; private workloads can remain behind a reachable origin tier.
scenes.narration: This network topology starts with CloudFront forwarding a cache miss or an uncached request to its application origin. In the illustrated ordinary custom-origin design, that endpoint is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The ALB listener accepts the CloudFront origin request and then forwards traffic to EC2 instances in private subnets. Notice the distinction: the application targets can be private while the origin endpoint remains reachable. The alternate public EC2 path makes the same requirement more obvious but increases direct server exposure. Security groups, listeners, protocols and origin certificates must be configured to fit the chosen path. CloudFront also supports separately configured VPC origins for eligible private resources; that is not the ordinary public custom-origin arrangement shown here. For a multi-tier application, use a reachable ALB as the controlled entry while leaving backend instances private. Do not confuse private target placement with automatic private connectivity from CloudFront.

scenes.title: Restrict direct ALB origin access
scenes.visual_overview: CloudFront-managed prefix list in ALB security group and a secret custom origin header checked by ALB listener rule; origin protection is layered.
visual_walkthrough: Examine the direct-to-ALB bypass attempt and the intended CloudFront-to-origin route
Use CloudFront-managed prefix lists in ALB security groups where supported
Explain an added custom origin header validated by ALB listener rules and its limitations
scenes.visual_example: A company wants users to access an ALB-hosted site through CloudFront and WAF rather than reaching the ALB directly; layered origin restrictions reduce bypass.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A secret origin header supplements network controls but does not alone create a private network boundary.
scenes.narration: This security-control diagram shows two request paths to the same ALB. The accepted path begins at CloudFront, where the viewer-facing controls can be applied, and proceeds to the ALB origin. The unwanted path is a client attempting to reach the ALB directly and bypass the distribution. One protection is to restrict allowed ALB source addresses using the AWS-managed CloudFront origin-facing prefix list where it fits the deployment. Another layer is a custom origin header sent by CloudFront and checked in an ALB listener rule. If the expected header is missing, the listener can reject the request. Neither technique should be mistaken for CloudFront viewer authorization by itself, and a header treated as a secret requires sound operational handling. In production, evaluate origin exposure, security groups and the actual threat model. The goal is to ensure the application's intended edge path cannot be trivially bypassed by direct requests.
